item.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading (117 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://honnibal.dev/blog/astra-read-write-misleading, See on Hacker News

Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working.

This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

If you read that, would you assume that the Qwen experiment worked ‘just by looking at the raw weights’? Well it doesn’t. In fact even the “small gameplaying network” experiment doesn’t work “just by looking at the raw weights”. There’s experiments that look at raw weights, and experiments that improve a game-playing network, and an experiment that improves Qwen at maths. But those latter two aren’t just looking at the raw weights.

Here’s a summary of what the post actually does and how the techniques work.

The “just by looking at the raw weights” setting (raw floats in context, no tools, no running the network) only appears in experiments 1, 2 and 4, on networks of 17K–172K weights. Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python, and the Qwen result, which is the headline one, also gets to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems.

What the Qwen result actually shows is that Astra can be prompted to devise and perform tasks that a human ML engineer could do. Human ML engineers write snippets of code that analyse or even modify network weights “directly” all the time. Figuring out how to do this productively is not nothing, and AI models of a year or two ago would have failed at all these tasks.

But to me the Qwen result and the other experiments that use Python don’t belong in the same post or paper as the experiments that read the weights directly. A single technique that could achieve both, “Author weights for a small game from scratch” and “Improve the performance of a large model on a sample task” would imply a deep capability. If you test a single technique that way you’ve demonstrated a sort of ‘gestalt’ of the weights (it can write them out from scratch) and also that it understands a large existing network. But that’s not at all true here, because it’s not a single technique.

item.title: Revolut moves to self-hosted GLM (149 pts)
item.description:

BREAKING: Revolut moved ~2,000 engineers onto self-hosted GLM for coding and pushed Claude Code and Codex to the exception list. Per David Abitbol, who leads AI ops there: 56 Nvidia B200s, a blended 30 cents per million tokens, roughly a tenth of what they paid Anthropic and OpenAI. Engineering lead time improved 70%. Here's the part that matters: the gains showed up when tokens stopped being rationed. Engineers quit saving AI for the hard tickets and pointed it at everything. Frontier models become the exception, open weights become the default. That's a pricing problem for every lab heading to IPO. h/t @OliverMolander Would you move your team off frontier APIs if the bill dropped 90%?

item.title: uBlock Origin filter to block autoplay videos in TechCrunch (111 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://cornfieldlabs.github.io/posts/ublock-stop-techcrunch-autoplay-video/post.html, See on Hacker News

cornfieldlabs

Every TechCrunch article autoplays a video in the middle of the post. Hiding it isn’t enough, because the player keeps running in the background.

The video is a JW Player embed, and the page also loads Connatix’s floating ad player. Blocking their scripts stops the video from loading at all, and the cosmetic rules hide the empty box it leaves behind.

These work in uBlock Origin on Firefox (the full MV2 version, not uBO Lite). Paste them into Dashboard → My filters and click Apply changes:

! TechCrunch: stop the autoplaying JW Player video
||content.jwplatform.com/libraries/$script,domain=techcrunch.com
||ssl.p.jwpcdn.com^$script,domain=techcrunch.com
||connatix.com^$third-party,domain=techcrunch.com
techcrunch.com##.wp-block-techcrunch-jw-player-embed
techcrunch.com##.jw-player-inline-promo

If TechCrunch switches video vendors, the ## rules will probably keep hiding the box, but you’ll need a new network rule to stop the audio.

item.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology (163 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology, See on Hacker News

Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.

It enables developers to:

  • Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
  • Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
  • Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
  • Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.

Benchmarks

To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository.

Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the Apache License 2.0. Third-party open-source components bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. This project is currently not accepting external contributions.

Key Features

  • Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
  • Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
  • Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth.
  • Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
  • Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack.

Software Components

Component Technology Role Default port
Frontend Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma Web UI, authentication, API gateway 3000
Backend FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs 3001
Ingestion worker FastAPI (Python 3.12+) Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings 3002
Postgres + pgvector Relational Database App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store 5432
HashiCorp Vault Optional Secure storage of connection credentials —

NVIDIA NIM

Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted NVIDIA API catalog (integrate.api.nvidia.com) or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:

  • LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
  • Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
  • Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2

The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT, DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL, EMBED_ENDPOINT, and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.

Model triplets

Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables — <PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY, and <PREFIX>_MODEL:

Prefix Role
DEFAULT_MODELS Shared default; every field below falls back to it.
REASONING Main chat / NL-to-SQL model.
NON_REASONING Lighter model used for entity extraction.
EMBED Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query).
RERANK Reranker used by the retrieval flow.

You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>. So the simplest setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL, NON_REASONING_MODEL). *_API_KEY also falls back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.

Deployment

Prerequisites

  • Docker with Docker Compose v2 (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows, Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see DEPLOYMENT.md.
  • An NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from the NVIDIA API catalog at https://build.nvidia.com.
  • Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query (Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB).

Installation

Kubernetes

To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see DEPLOYMENT.md.

Local (Docker Compose)

  1. Clone the repository:

    git clone <repo-url> auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology

  2. Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values (Postgres credentials, DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY, CONNECTION_STRINGS, etc.). See .env.example for the full list of variables:

    cp .env.example .env
# edit .env

    Note:

    • AUTH_SECRET and APP_URL are required — without them every page fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error.
    • POSTGRES_PORT only changes the host-side port mapping (set it if 5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres on the internal network port.

  3. Build the images and start the stack:

    docker compose up -d --build

    This builds the backend (auto_ontology) and frontend (auto-ontology-frontend) images, brings up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot frontend-migrate job to sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service, and frontend).

  4. Open the UI at http://localhost:3000 (the backend API is on :3001, pgAdmin on :5050).

    Troubleshooting: if the UI loads without the left navigation panel (or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a stale session cookie — this happens when AUTH_SECRET changes or the database is reset. Clear the site data for localhost:3000 (or delete the better-auth.session_token cookie) and sign in again.

Connections Management

Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources:

  1. Added through the UI — connections created from within the app. With this option the connection credentials are stored in plaintext in Postgres unless Vault is configured:

    • Without Vault: the full connection object (including the password) is JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row.
    • With Vault: the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the lookup key — there is no separate reference field).

    Vault is enabled only when all of VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_NAMESPACE, VAULT_ROLE_ID, and VAULT_SECRET_ID are set (VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT and VAULT_KV_MOUNT are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage.

  2. CONNECTION_STRINGS environment variable — a comma-separated list of connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm --set connectionStrings=<CONNECTION-STRINGS> flag). This is a fallback: it is used only when there are no UI-added connections.

Authentication

Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication. The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback

API tokens (scripting)

A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an API token instead:

  1. Open the user menu (top right) → API Tokens → New token.
  2. Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and copy the token. Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it means minting a new one.

Send it as x-api-key on any /api/... call — Authorization: Bearer <token> works too:

curl -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms
import os
import requests

session = requests.Session()
session.headers["x-api-key"] = os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]

terms = session.get("https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms").json()

answer = session.post(
    "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions",
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
).json()

Things worth knowing:

  • A token acts as its owner. It carries no permissions of its own — every call is authorized against the owner's role, exactly as it would be in the browser. A viewer's token cannot do admin things.
  • The whole API surface accepts it. Authentication is resolved in one place (frontend/auth/resolve-user.ts) for every route, so any endpoint in docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json that is not withPublic works with a token.
  • Revocation is immediate. Delete the token in the UI, or delete/ban the owning user, and the next request with it gets a 401.
  • Tokens cannot manage tokens. Creating and revoking requires a signed-in session, so a leaked token cannot issue itself successors.

Agent API conversations

Public clients call the authenticated Next.js gateway at POST /api/chat/completions. The response is an SSE stream containing step, result, or error events, followed by [DONE].

conversation_id is optional:

  • Omit it for a stateless, one-shot request.
  • Supply a client-generated UUID to create or continue a conversation.
  • Reuse the same UUID for every turn in the thread. Wait for [DONE] before sending the next turn; overlapping requests for one conversation return 409 Conversation in progress.
{
  "question": "What about last month?",
  "conversation_id": "d61d8aa3-d496-4fa7-97ce-4f831c162e7f"
}

For conversational requests, FastAPI loads up to the five most recent completed turns (bounded to 12,000 characters) and rewrites contextual input such as “What about August?” into a standalone question before running the existing text-to-SQL graph. Independent questions are passed through unchanged. Internal agent thoughts, chart payloads, errors, and raw SQL result sets are not reused as context.

Conversation history is scoped to the authenticated Auto Ontology user. Browser and service callers should use the Next.js gateway, which resolves the user and forwards the internal x-auto-ontology-user-id header to FastAPI. The FastAPI port is a trusted internal service boundary: it must not be exposed publicly because that header is not independently verified by FastAPI. A direct FastAPI request without conversation_id remains stateless; a direct request with conversation_id requires the trusted identity header.

The web UI manages the UUID automatically. An API-created conversation can be opened in the UI at /chat?focus=<conversation_id> when it belongs to the signed-in user.

Agent skills

Coding agents: start at AGENTS.md. Skills live in skills/ (nvidia-ontology-setup, nvidia-ontology-management, nvidia-ontology-query). Maintainers keep using CLAUDE.md.

MCP server

Agent harnesses such as Cursor and Claude Desktop can query your data through Auto Ontology's MCP server. See mcp/ to run it and docs/mcp.md for the details.

License

Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form:

All rights reserved.

Third-party open-source components used by Auto Ontology are enumerated, with their upstream licenses and project URLs, in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Components added by the container images are listed separately in CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk.

External materials Auto Ontology interacts with at run time:

Material When Terms

Contributing

This project is currently not accepting contributions. Issues, pull requests, and patches submitted from outside the Auto Ontology maintainer team will not be reviewed or merged. Researchers Report Direct Edits to Neural-Network Weights

An MIT CSAIL team reports early experiments in which GPT-6 Astra interpreted and modified neural-network weights without writing a training loop. In one Qwen test, the authors say a small weight change sharply improved math and instruction-following scores; the findings are preliminary.

Andrej Karpathy Builds a Video Library From Hacker News Recommendations

HackerTube gathers 6,454 YouTube videos mentioned by Hacker News readers across nearly two decades. Karpathy describes using AI coding tools to build an alternative browsing experience, with its own recommendations and no user accounts.

PostgreSQL Developer Links Release Delay to AI-Found Bugs

Robert Haas attributes the delayed release to a growing backlog of AI-assisted bug reports. He describes late feature reversions and the human review still required to turn suggested fixes into reliable code.

Readers Search for a Television That Respects Their Privacy

US boy names that became girl names and vice versa

The linked article was unavailable during this update. This is the original Hacker News submission title; no article summary or image is included.

The conversation

Technology

An Archivist’s Plea: Save the Websites You Love

After a longtime fan site vanished, a web archivist makes the case for personal backups. The post walks through capture and replay tools, with a disclosure that the author works for the company behind them.

Software

An Earlier Report Questions Ubuntu’s Kernel-Patch Delay

In an October 31 article, freenode news reported that Ubuntu’s 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 LTS releases still lacked kernels patched for CVE-2026-98432. This is the report’s account, not a fresh verification of Canonical’s current patch status.

An Argument for Mathematics Beyond Individual Credit

In a guest essay on Terence Tao’s blog, Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai and Jie Xue argue that mathematical work should be valued for the understanding it brings, not for outperforming other people or machines. They urge a less ego-centered response to AI’s role in research.

The project presents a three-dimensional model of central Warsaw assembled from OpenStreetMap, LiDAR and the city’s tree database, with a voxel resolution of one meter.

In a Microsoft blog recollection, the author describes slipping into an early rehearsal and learning that Patrick Stewart would host the Windows 2000 launch. A headset-wearing crew member stood in for the actor during the run-through.

item.title: DiscImageStudio: burn visible artwork onto CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs (285 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/JiaFeiMiao-K-Cat/DiscImageStudio, See on Hacker News

简体中文 | 繁體中文 | English | 日本語

全能的光盘盘面可见图像生成与刻录工具

Windows 桌面版支持设计与刻录，Linux 和 macOS 的实验性命令行版可离线生成 CD、DVD 和蓝光镜像。

效果预览

概述

Disc Image Studio 可将一张图片转换成符合 CD、DVD 与单层 BD-R 光盘物理层约束的数据，刻录后将使光盘盘面呈现肉眼可见的图案。

界面预览

快速开始

Windows 下载 win-x64.exe 后可直接运行。Linux 或 macOS 请下载与 CPU 匹配的实验性 CLI 压缩包，解压后运行 ./disc-image-studio --help。这些发布包均自带 .NET 运行时。 GitHub Releases

1. 新建工程

在主页选择 CD、DVD 或蓝光，指定输出位置后创建工程。

2. 设计盘面

在设计页导入图片，用图层完成排版，并在右栏「影调」模块调整抖动、伽马、亮度与灰阶档位。

3. 预览与导出

在预览页核对盘面投影，在导出页生成 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE，或使用即时刻录功能直接写入空白盘片。

即时刻录为实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。

功能

光盘数据生成

  • CD 支持：支持任何 CD 。您可导出带格式头的 WAV 音轨及配套 CUE，兼容 cdrecord, ImgBurn等刻录软件；也允许导出 RAW 音轨。详见 CD 刻录兼容说明。
  • DVD 支持：支持任何 DVD。您可导出 ISO 镜像。
  • 蓝光支持：支持任何单层 BD-R 25 GB，支持纯绘图与 UDF 2.01 文件。详见 ADDING_BLURAY.md。
  • 随盘文件：CD／DVD／蓝光可在设计页直接选择要保存的文件夹及内圈／外圈位置，也可在导出页调整；设置随工程保存。
  • 文件区域预览：混合盘的设计投影和成品读回用黄色标出文件区（含文件系统）。
  • 介质灰度方案：CD 与 DVD 均使用黑白二阶，CD 使用 0D / AA，DVD 扰码域使用 A5 / 92。详见 PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md。
  • 灰度抖动工具：独立程序也可将原图处理为 0/255 黑白二阶 PNG；支持打开或拖入原图、并排预览及无损 PNG 导出。详见使用与构建说明。
  • 盘片预设：内置数个品牌的光盘参数，覆盖 CD／DVD／BD。您也可将自己标定好的数据贡献给我们，详见预设维护说明。

辅助标定

Disc Image Studio 提供了一套智能且精准的辅助标定流程，相较人工肉眼识别标定，辅助标定算法将可确定的盘面物理数据精确度从 10-6 提升到了 10-14。校准前采用恒定轨距，十字线的径向线条出现明显弯曲；使用辅助标定得到的三次轨距参数重新生成并刻录后，线条更接近径向直线。

流程与参数说明见辅助标定说明。

刻录

  • 镜像文件输出：您可以导出完整 ISO / RAW 文件并使用合适的刻录软件手动刻录。
  • 即时流式刻录（实验性）：CD、DVD 与 BD-R 边生成边刻录，不保存完整镜像；BD-R 走 MMC 顺序写入。
  • 不要使用非空白介质！

应用形态

  • 多语言界面：点击右上角「设置」按钮，在「通用 → 语言」选择简体中文、繁體中文、English、日本語或跟随系统，保存并重启应用后生效。语言和主题默认均跟随系统，已保存的明确选择继续保留；跟随系统时区分简体和繁体中文，日文系统使用日文，其他系统语言使用英文。
  • 双入口：不带参数将打开 GUI；带参数则进入统一命令行。
  • 模块化：CD、DVD 与蓝光通过 IOpticalDiscModule 接入，统一命令目录与任务契约，详见架构说明。

系统与设备要求

  • 桌面版需要 Windows 10 2004（2004/20H1，19041）及以上，或 Windows 11。
  • 构建：.NET 10 SDK（global.json 锁定 10.0.x）；自行构建的非自包含 GUI 需要 .NET 10 Windows 桌面运行时。Release EXE 已包含运行时，无需另行安装 .NET。
  • “即时刻录”功能需要一台 Windows 可识别的 CD / DVD / BD 刻录机与空白盘片；BD-R 需要支持顺序写入的单层空白盘。

构建与运行

dotnet build DiscImageStudio.slnx --configuration Release
dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.App --configuration Release

构建回归检查：

dotnet run --project src/DvdImageSolver --configuration Release -- selftest
dotnet run --project tests/DiscImageStudio.ArchitectureTests --configuration Release

版本规则、CI 生成 EXE、Release 草稿检查、MSIX 打包与签名流程见发布指南。

命令行

Linux（glibc）可选 linux-x64 或 linux-arm64。Apple Silicon Mac 选 osx-arm64，Intel Mac 选 osx-x64。CLI 在本地生成镜像，实际写盘可交给支持相应镜像或音轨的刻录软件。

使用 .NET 10 SDK 从源码运行 CLI

dotnet run --project src/DiscImageStudio.Cli -c Release -- --help

CLI 可读取 PNG、JPEG、BMP 和 GIF，使用动画图片的第一帧。下面的例子用两扇区音轨验证安装，同时生成配套 CUE。

./disc-image-studio cd-generate --input picture.png --output sample.wav --sectors 2
命令 说明
solve 使用固定快速纹理映射（CW 方向）生成 DVD 镜像，黑白纹理可选抖动混合
encode 将单个 DVD ECC 块编码为 NRZI 通道电平
calibrate 标定投影：按生成几何从 DVD 源图片取样，按实测几何投到盘面
simulate 按实测半径对生成的 DVD ISO 做读回模拟
selftest 运行 DVD 引擎的确定性回归自检
cd-generate 无随盘文件时生成 WAV + CUE / RAW 音轨；指定 --data-dir 时生成 CD 数据盘 ISO
cd-preview-warp 标定投影：按实测几何投影 CD 源图片
cd-preview-track 按标定几何渲染已有的 WAV 或 RAW CD-DA 音轨（读回模拟）
bd-generate 生成完整 BD-R ISO，并写出 <iso>.json sidecar
bd-info / bd-probe / bd-encode 导出 BD 参数、原始负载探针或单个 ECC 簇诊断

源码结构

src/DiscImageStudio.ImageIO/ WIC 和跨平台图像编解码
src/DiscImageStudio.Core/    介质无关的模块契约、工程/预设模型、任务与命令目录
src/DiscImageStudio.Imaging/ CD/DVD/BD 共用的图片预处理与抖动辅助

src/DiscImageStudio.Cd/      CD-DA 生成核心与 CD 模块
src/DiscImageStudio.Dvd/     DVD 引擎适配模块
src/DiscImageStudio.BluRay/  BD-R 几何、17PP/ECC、3T/6T 映射、流式生成与 ISO

src/DiscImageStudio.App/     WPF GUI、统一命令行与商店资源
src/DvdImageSolver/          保持隔离的 DVD 编码/求解引擎
tests/                       无第三方测试框架的架构回归测试
packaging/                   MSIX 清单与打包脚本
tools/                       独立辅助工具与资产生成脚本
docs/                        架构、引擎、预设、发布等文档

文档

文档 内容
ARCHITECTURE.md 模块抽象、层间边界与扩展规则
LOCALIZATION.md 界面语言配置、系统语言回退与翻译资源维护

CD_AUDIO_COMPATIBILITY.md CD 音轨格式、字节序与重影排查
ADDING_BLURAY.md 蓝光模块的物理模型、生成/刻录链路与扩展点
DISC_PRESETS.md 可编辑盘片预设的分层 JSON 格式与合并规则
CALIBRATION.md 照片矫正（框选盘片实体最外缘与中心孔边缘）、曲线标定与 DVD 三次轨距拟合
PHYSICAL_MODEL_AUDIT.md CD / DVD 生成物理模型复核
VALIDATION.md 各轮构建、回归与实盘测试的本地验证记录
RELEASING.md GitHub Release、MSIX 打包、签名测试与商店提交流程
CHANGELOG.md 版本变更记录

参考标准

Disc Image Studio 的实现与物理模型主要参考以下规范：

介质 标准与版本 本项目采用的范围
CD-R ECMA-394，第 1 版，2010 年 12 月 — Recordable Compact Disc Systems CD-R Multi-Speed（官方 PDF） CD-R 介质、多速录制及 CD-DA 兼容关系；本项目生成 CD-DA 音轨。
DVD 公共格式 / DVD-ROM ECMA-267，第 3 版，2001 年 4 月 — 120 mm DVD – Read-only disk（官方 PDF） DVD 数据帧、ECC、EFMPlus 编码及附录 G 转换表；可记录盘的介质规则另参考 ECMA-359。
DVD-R ECMA-359，第 1 版，2004 年 12 月 — 80 mm (1,46 Gbytes per side) and 120 mm (4,70 Gbytes per side) DVD Recordable Disk (DVD-R)（官方 PDF） 单层 DVD-R 的几何、扇区、纠错和编码；标准包含单面及双面介质，双面不等于双层。
BD-R ISO/IEC 30190:2021，第 3 版，2021 年 1 月 — 120 mm 单层（25.0 GB）及双层（50.0 GB）可记录 BD 的信息交换与存储规范 实验模式采用单层 25 GB 的轨道、扇区布局、纠错和编码；目前不支持双层盘。

CD 公共编码部分还参考了 ECMA-130，第 2 版（CD-ROM，1996）。

刻录与介质安全须知

  • Disc Image Studio 不安装驱动或服务；“即时刻录”功能使用了 Windows 自带的 IMAPI2，拒绝非空白介质。
  • “即时刻录”功能已有部分实盘反馈，对不同设备、介质与刻录入口的验证覆盖仍有限，属于实验性功能，请只使用可报废的测试介质。刻录中断、断电或生成速度不足仍可能使盘片报废！
  • 实际可见效果取决于盘片、刻录机、固件与写入策略。
  • 混合文件夹会在开始刻录前扫描目录并固定布局；期间源文件大小改变会安全终止任务，已开始写入的盘片仍可能报废。
  • BD-R 顺序写入不提供备用区重映射；中断后同一盘片通常不能继续写入。

隐私与安全

  • Disc Image Studio 不联网、不上传文件、不收集遥测，详见隐私政策。
  • 发现安全问题请不要在公开 Issue 中披露，按安全政策使用 GitHub 私密报告。

贡献

欢迎报告问题与提交代码。开发环境搭建、模块边界规则、测试要求与 Pull Request 流程见贡献指南。

许可证

项目采用 GNU GPL v3.0 or later（GPL-3.0-or-later）。CD 交织实现包含从 CDImage 移植并修改的代码，整体分发沿用兼容的 GPL 授权；分发二进制或修改版时须遵守对应源代码等要求。第三方字体与组件遵循各自许可证，详见 授权说明 和 第三方声明；应用"关于"页也可离线查看完整文本。

致谢

感谢 arduinocelentano 的 CDImage 项目，它展示了通过生成 CD 音轨在盘面形成可见图像的方法。本项目的 CD 交织实现由其相关代码移植并继续修改，CD 盘面绘图思路也受其启发。CDImage 原作者及贡献者的工作为本项目提供了重要基础。

item.title: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads (216 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-intel-stock-collapse-is-getting-worse--and-the-37-trillion-chip-rout-is-spreading-212154947.html, See on Hacker News

Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house.

About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Intel (INTC) led the way down again.

The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended.

And the damage didn't stick to Intel.

Micron (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), Seagate (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell (MRVL) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum (LITE) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia (NVDA) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6.

Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants.

Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX (SPCX) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet (FTNT) and CrowdStrike (CRWD), which fell with chips.

Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst.

"The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom."

John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening.

"There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia."

Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term "Octoberphobia," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%.

Next up is AMD (AMD), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell, the same day as the midterm vote.

item.title: Anthropic's growth just flattened (217 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.regenerator1.com/p/anthropics-growth-just-flattened, See on Hacker News

Anthropic shared high-level Q3 financials with investors yesterday, report the NYT’s Andrew Ross Sorkin, Lauren Hirsch, and Sri Muppidi.

Revenue for Q3 was reportedly $16.8 billion.

At first glance, this number seems astonishing. And, in one sense, it is. It’s another jaw-dropping sequential gain for what is likely the fastest-growing company in history.

But, break the trend down into implied monthly growth, and the picture looks different.

Specifically, it seems Anthropic barely grew from July to September.

Anthropic’s sequential revenue growth in Q3, moreover, was smaller in absolute dollars than its (gobsmacking) growth in Q2.

So, for several possible reasons, Anthropic’s growth has meaningfully slowed.

This is likely another reason why the stocks of “neocloud” providers like CoreWeave are collapsing. CoreWeave, et al, have borrowed tens of billions of dollars on the assumption that demand for AI compute will continue to grow at rates way beyond consensus expectations for years.

Now, not only are interest rates soaring — raising the carrying costs of this debt — the near-term revenue growth for AI services may be flattening.

Anthropic’s reported revenue growth this year has been unprecedented:

Q1: $4.8 billion
Q2: $11.6 billion (+$6.8B and +141%, sequentially)
Q3: $16.8 billion (+$5.2B and +45%, sequentially)

Again, these numbers are astonishing.

But so are AI valuations and expectations.

Note that Anthropic added more revenue in Q2 than it did in Q3.

Note, too, that what matters most for Anthropic’s IPO valuation — and, likely, for the future trajectory of the AI bubble — is not what has happened but what will happen.

The key question is, “What do these numbers suggest about how fast Anthropic will grow from here?”

These figures suggest that the market should temper its expectations, at least temporarily.

If we break down the quarterly figures above into monthly estimates and add one more reported data point — that Anthropic had a $65 billion annualized revenue run-rate in July — we see that Anthropic’s growth has flattened even more than the quarterly figures suggest.

Below are back-of-the-envelope estimates for Anthropic’s monthly revenue in 2026. They are based on the reported quarterly revenue figures as well as the $65 billion annualized revenue in July (which equates to ~$5.4 billion of July revenue).

Even the quarterly numbers suggest that Anthropic’s average monthly growth slowed from ~$760 million in Q2 to (“only”) $580 million a month in Q3.

But the “$65 billion annualized revenue in July” data point suggests the slowdown is even sharper.

If Anthropic did $5.4 billion in revenue in July and $16.8 billion in Q3, it likely only grew modestly in August and September.

According to DealBook, at its meeting with investors yesterday, Anthropic did not share an annualized revenue number based on September’s revenue. This suggests — to this analyst, anyway — that Anthropic did not think the September annualized revenue figure would show impressive-enough growth versus July.

Indeed, when we extrapolate the monthly figures, it seems Anthropic saw a sharp change in its growth trajectory in August and September.

It means that the growth of the leading company in the sector appears to have slowed sharply in the past two months.

The slowdown might at least in part be the result of seasonality. August, at least, tends to be a slow month. But it’s early in a product cycle to see such sharp seasonality. And September’s growth should have sped back up.

It might also mean that Anthropic is simply not able to keep up with the growth of demand. If this is the reason for the slowdown, it’s a high-quality problem, and it won’t have a long-term impact on the overall AI spending growth trajectory (or bubble).

But it may also mean that the near-term growth rate of AI spending is moderating — either because demand growth is moderating or because companies are using cheaper models from China for some of their AI needs. (Usage data suggests the latter is in fact happening).

If a slowdown in spending growth is the explanation, we should expect the wild investor enthusiasm for all things AI — and the colossal infrastructure spending growth supporting it — to also begin to moderate.

The end of all bubbles comes when supply begins to catch up with demand.

Anthropic’s apparent slowdown suggests we may be closer to reaching that moment.

item.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public (372 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.techpolicy.press/the-sec-should-block-anthropics-ipo-to-protect-the-public/, See on Hacker News

Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts.

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.

That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.

The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.

Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.

Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.

The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.

Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense: they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.

Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts, Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.

Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.

Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins

AI industry margins

Demand pressure:

Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI.

Commoditization:

Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices.

Cost pressures:

High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash.

External constraints:

Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation.

First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies, including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).

Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid.

Our content delivered to your inbox.

Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.

In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.

That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion, and the prices for some components are soaring.

That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.

And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.

Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.

Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.

If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.

It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect.” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.

The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy.

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.

Electrek’s Take

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025.

Justin Sullivan | Getty Images

Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.

The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.

"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."

Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.

Oracle's one-day performance

The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.

"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.

Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.

Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.

The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.

Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.

What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.

"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."

— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

item.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era (173 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/11/02/egoless-mathematics-in-the-ai-era/, See on Hacker News

[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.

There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.

While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.

The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.

The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.

Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.

The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?

Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.

Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.

From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.

The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.

This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.

This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI, but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all. Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.

Seen in this light, we need not be afraid of what AI may achieve in mathematics. Mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born, and it will remain beautiful long after we are gone. Its worth does not depend on our accomplishments, nor does our joy in understanding it have to depend on being the ones who make the discoveries. Our purpose rests on our willingness to let truth govern what we seek and what we become.

We, the authors of this essay, are still far from having attained such egolessness. Nevertheless, we recognize it as an ideal toward which we wish to strive.

We conclude with a thought experiment. Ramanujan is reported to have said, “An equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God” (Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity, 1992). If he were alive today, witnessing the advances of AI in mathematics, would he be perturbed by what they might mean for his purpose as a mathematician?

item.title: Ballot Rejections Have Soared in Rural Counties as USPS Reduces Mail Service (107 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-ballot-delays-postal-service-midterms, See on Hacker News

Reporting Highlights

  • Rural Cuts: Delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, a ProPublica analysis found.
  • Rejected Ballots: The rates of ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in areas affected by the cuts compared to the 2022 primary. That wasn’t the case elsewhere.
  • Extraordinary Measures: Postal Service leaders say special procedures in place for the Nov. 3 election should prevent similar delays, but experts warn that mistakes are likely.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.

Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.

Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.

In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail. 

But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.

Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.

The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers. 

In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.

In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed. 

Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.

Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting. 

“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”

Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service

Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.

At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system. 

“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”

Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely. 

“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'”

A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)

After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.

At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.

Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.

“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.

The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006. 

When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)

The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since. 

Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.

The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.

Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024 Election

A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.

In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.

This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.

Mail Service Has Been Cut in Large Swaths of Rural America

A plan to reduce mail pickup frequency is being rolled out in ZIP codes that are more than 50 miles from a sorting facility. Areas not subject to the plan are mostly in or near large cities.

Mail Service Has Been Cut in Large Swaths of Rural America

A plan to reduce mail pickup frequency is being rolled out in ZIP codes that are more than 50 miles from a sorting facility. Areas not subject to the plan are mostly in or near large cities.

Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.

A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.

“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”

Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.

In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.

In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.

Has Mail Service Been Reduced in Your ZIP Code?

If the frequency of mail pickups has been reduced in your area, mail may take longer to send and receive, and the date on the postmark could be later than the day you dropped it off, which may matter for mail like ballots that is subject to a deadline.

In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.

“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”

In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.

Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.

Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.

Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.

Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.

The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.

ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.) 

Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect. 

“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher. 

Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.

A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.

In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.

Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen. 

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.

“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

No patched kernels are available yet for 22.04, 24.04, or 26.04 despite a CVSS 9.8 rating.

Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432, a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update.

Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables.

Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

Abstract:Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%.
